Before the city wakes, there is a brief blue silence when every window seems possible, and even the streets appear to be listening with me. I like that hour because nothing has yet become an errand, and the ordinary world still carries the soft authority of a secret worth keeping.

A baker lifts a shutter somewhere, and the first warm loaves send their invisible messages through empty lanes still silver with rain from last night. A cat crosses the road without hurrying, certain that whoever matters will wait, while a single bird practices one clear note, then carefully tries another.

We often speak as though wonder requires distance, mountains, tickets, or some grand permission, but it usually begins with simply staying awake to our lives. The cup warming my hands, the uneven chair, and the familiar face across the table are small, temporary, and quietly astonishing when I notice them.

Perhaps attention is a form of affection, a way of telling ordinary things they do not need to shine before we offer them our care. By noon, the spell will not be broken, only hidden beneath voices, engines, lists, and the bright insistence that real life is happening somewhere else.

Still, evening returns what morning offered, and the sky again becomes patient enough to hold every color we failed to name during the loud day. If I can carry one unnoticed beauty through the noise, then tomorrow may find me gentler, less hungry for spectacle, more at home than before.
